question.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Their Components
question.problem: Find the angle between $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
question.worked_solution:
Rearranging the dot product formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 6+7\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{7}^{2}}\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{19}{\sqrt{53}\cdot \sqrt{37}} \\  & =\frac{19}{\sqrt{1961}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{19}{\sqrt{1961}})≈{64.6}^{∘}.
$$

question.problem: Find the angle between $a=⟨4,-3,2⟩$ and $b=⟨3,4,1⟩.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Rearranging the dot product formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3+(-3)\cdot 4+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}\cdot \sqrt{26}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{754}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{2}{\sqrt{754}})≈{85.82}^{∘}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Three Points
question.problem: Find $∠BAC$ given the points $A(2,-1,1)$, $B(3,1,-2)$, and $C(-1,1,1).$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
question.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨2,-1,1⟩,\,b=⟨3,1,-2⟩,\,c=⟨-1,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3,1,-2⟩-⟨2,-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2,-3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨-1,1,1⟩-⟨2,-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-3)+2\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}\cdot \sqrt{13}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{182}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{182}})≈{86}^{∘}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Three Points
question.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $P$, $Q$, $R$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}p=⟨-4,3,1⟩,\,q=⟨-1,2,0⟩,\,r=⟨-10,5,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The $△PQR$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠QPR=\theta .$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/3003f0cb329a8f8ef9bc315c70df4773ac1f0c54843dea1208c68bd0f6227bd1.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =q-p \\  & =⟨-1,2,0⟩-⟨-4,3,1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-1,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =⟨-10,5,3⟩-⟨-4,3,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot \overset{\to }{PR}}{|\overset{\to }{PQ}||\overset{\to }{PR}|} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot (-6)+(-1)\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-22}{\sqrt{11}\cdot \sqrt{44}} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-1)={180}^{∘}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given the Value of Their Dot Product
question.problem: Given that $p\cdot q=-5$, find the angle between $p=⟨4t,-2,t⟩$ and $q=⟨1,3,-3⟩.$ Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
question.worked_solution:
First, since $p\cdot q=-5$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =-5 \\ 4t\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 3+t\cdot (-3) & =-5 \\ 4t-6-3t & =-5 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨4(1),-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $p$ and $q$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,p\,||\,q\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{\sqrt{{p}_{x}^{2}+{p}_{y}^{2}+{p}_{z}^{2}}\sqrt{{q}_{x}^{2}+{q}_{y}^{2}+{q}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-5}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{21}\cdot \sqrt{19}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{399}}.\end{aligned}
$$

THerefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{399}})≈{104.5}^{∘}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given the Value of Their Dot Product
question.problem: Given that $a\cdot b=-10$, find the angle between $a=⟨-4t,3t⟩$ and $b=⟨2,1⟩.$ Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
question.worked_solution:
First, since $a\cdot b=-10$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =-10 \\ (-4t)\cdot 2+3t\cdot 1 & =-10 \\ -8t+3t & =-10 \\ -5t & =-10 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨-4(2),\,3(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $a$ and $b$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-10}{\sqrt{(-8)^{2}+{6}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{10}{10\cdot \sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})≈{116.6}^{∘}.
$$
